title: System Design

sentences.text: Welcome to the NPTEL MOOC's course on Foundations of Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems.
We are going to start a new lecture on the design part: design of immersive experiences.
So, earlier we talked about methods for user requirement gathering.
So, earlier we talked about how to gather usability requirements, or in other words, end user requirements.
And also how that idea was used in our case study, in particular how we identified issues that are relevant to be addressed to make our Majuli VR Tour usable.
In this lecture, what we are going to do is basically learn about designing the experience, particularly interface and interaction design.
If we quickly have a relook or if we quickly recap the interactive system development lifecycle, the stages, you can see there are several stages.

Feasibility study, starting with feasibility study, then requirement gathering, analysis and specification, then this design prototype and evaluate cycle comprising design, prototyping and early evaluation.
Then we have code design, followed by coding and implementation, followed by code testing, which is followed by empirical study or empirical testing or usability testing.
Finally, deployment and maintenance.
In between, there are lots of feedback loops.
So, one between here, then we have this loop, then we have this loop, then we also have this loop.
So, a lot of feedback loops are there.
Out of these, we have already talked about the requirement gathering stage.
Note that there are two design stages: one is the design mentioned in this part, and the other one is code design.
So, here we are going to talk about the design stage of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, particularly related to interface and code design, interface, and interaction design.
Interface plus interaction design.
So, we are going to talk about that part in this lecture.
So, SDLC includes code and system design as well.
However, we will not focus on code design here.
Again, I am assuming, like in the case of functional requirements, I am assuming that you are already familiar with that stage or how it is done.
And here, in the case of interactive system development lifecycle also, it is the same as in any other software.
So, there is no difference between code design here and code design for any non-interactive software development as well.
So, we are not going to separately discuss that.
So, let us start with the basic concepts of design.
as in interface and interaction design.
So, when we talk of experience, designing the experience, the immersive experience, it involves the entire design-prototype-evaluate cycle in order to incorporate the user requirements.
Now, in this lecture, we are going to focus on the design part.
In the next lecture, In a separate lecture, we will be talking about the two components, namely prototype and evaluation.
So, here in this lecture, our focus will be only on the design part.
Now, when we talk of design, design of interface and interaction, there are two issues.
First is where to start, how do we start the design process, and how to represent whatever we have designed.
In other words, we can say we need to have a design language to express our design.
The first thing is to start the process, and the second thing is, whenever we are coming up with a design, how to express it so that we can brainstorm on it or we can refine it.
Let us first talk about where to start.
Of course, generally it is assumed that this is part of a creative thinking process.
So, we can rely on our creativity, which may be aided by intuition.

Also, it can be aided by experience or domain knowledge; that is, of course, if we have nothing to rely on, then we can rely on our creativity, which can be aided by our intuition and/or the expertise or experience or domain knowledge.
It can also start with some guidelines.
So, we can also think of starting the process based on some guidelines or thumb rules or checklists or heuristics.
These are known by different names.
So, those can act as a starting point to aid our creative thinking.
So, of course, interface interaction design requires creativity and imagination.
Along with that, we can take recourse to some guidelines, often called checklists, heuristics, thumb rules, and so on.
Now, there are many such guidelines.
Some are very generic and consequently small in size.
They are very broad in nature and the number of guidelines is generally small.
So, they cover broad aspects of interactive systems at a rather high level.
Examples are eight golden rules by Shneiderman, primarily meant to take care of graphical user interfaces, but those are so generic that they can be applicable to other cases as well.
Similarly, the seven principles by Norman.
Donald Norman.
Again, it was designed in the 1980s, developed in the 1980s, primarily meant for GUIs, but again because of the generic nature, it can be applied to other domains as well.
There are other more detailed and specific sets of guidelines available.
They are generally large in number because they cover micro details of a particular system.
So, to cover minute aspects of the design, they are generally large in number and they are typically meant for specific products.
For example, the human interface guidelines originally developed by Apple for their user interfaces.
That is the starting point.
So we can start with our creativity aided by experience or intuition or some guidelines.
We can even rely on all three.
Then there is this language.
How do we express whatever we are thinking?
So this essentially refers to a specification of design.
Note that earlier we talked of specification of requirements.
Now we are talking of specification of design.
There can be different languages for specifying the design.
And generally specification of interface design, the language used to specify interface design is likely to be different than the language used to specify code design.
Now to express interface and interaction design ideas, we can take recourse to prototypes.
Now, a prototype, in a sense, can be thought of as a language to express our design ideas.
So, it can be considered a language for interface design.
However, we will talk about this language in the next lecture, not as part of this lecture.
In a subsequent lecture, we will talk about prototypes for interactive systems, different categories, and how they can be utilized.
Let us now talk about the starting point: how do we start the design? We have our creativity, we have our imagination, but along with that, we can make use of design guidelines.
So, let us talk about design guidelines.
So, as mentioned earlier, we have specific guidelines as well as generic guidelines.
In an earlier lecture, if you can refer to module 1, lecture number 12, we learned about some specific guidelines to be followed for avoiding or minimizing cyber sickness.
These are typically applicable for VR or immersive systems where immersion is a very important issue.
Now, since in AR, the notion of immersion is different than that applicable for VR, those cyber sickness guidelines may not be specifically applicable for AR systems.
So, that is an example of a specific guideline set.
In this case, it is VR-specific guidelines to avoid cyber sickness, one specific aspect of VR.
Also, we can talk about generic guidelines, which are applicable for any interactive system, including XR systems.
Later on, we will see that they may not be fully applicable, but mostly applicable to extended reality systems.
So, let us talk about one such generic guideline, that is the Eight Golden Rules by Ben Shneiderman.
Now, as I mentioned earlier, it was originally developed in 1986 about 40 years back and it was primarily meant for GUIs, graphical user interfaces.
It is a set of eight rules or guidelines.
It can be partly or fully applicable to other types of interfaces as well, including extended reality systems.
Once we go through the guidelines, you can judge for yourself whether these are applicable to any extended reality systems.
Let us talk about the eight rules that are part of the golden rules of Shneiderman.
Let us start with rule number one, which says to strive for consistency.
So, whenever you are designing systems, an interface, you should always strive for consistency.
There must be consistency in your design.
What does it mean?
There are two types of consistency.
One is internal, one is external or environmental consistency.

Internal means whatever elements, whatever interactions that you are using in one part of the design for specific tasks, the same thing should be utilized in other parts of the design for the same task.
So, in different designs, in different usage instances for the same tasks, separate objects, separate elements, or separate interactions should not be utilized. That is internal consistency.
There is something called external consistency as well, that is.
So, whenever we are using a system, we come with some real-world knowledge.
So, when we are using a system, that knowledge should be as closely matching with our experience with the virtual world as possible.
So, real-world knowledge transfer to the virtual world should be as close as possible.
That means the elements that we deal with, the interactions that we perform, should be close to our real-world experience as much as possible.
So, that is consistency, external consistency.
Rule number two is design for universal usability.
So, if you recollect earlier, we talked about knowing the user, and we also talked about a broad categorization of users.
We saw that there are three broad classes of users.
novice, intermittent, and expert.
Novice means first time user, first time user.
Intermittent refers to occasional users, and expert refers to frequent users.
Now, note that here the term expert does not mean expert in technology, rather expert in usage of the system.
Now, typically when we design, we should have facilities for all classes of users.
Let us take one example.
So, we all have used some sort of word processor.
to type, to save text, to create text documents, to save text documents, and so on.
Now, suppose we are using such a word processor system to create a text document, and we want to save it.
Now, saving can be done with hotkeys, that is a combination of keys.
Say, for example, Ctrl plus S.
that can be used to save a document.
Also, we can save a document using a menu option like save.
Now, why to keep both the options in a single system?
The reason is one option is meant for One type of user, another option is meant for another type of user.
Those who are experts, they typically do not want to use menu-based options because that is slower.
So, they will be going for hotkeys or the Control plus S option which is faster.
Whereas, those who are novices or intermittent, they may not remember the hotkey combinations.
So, for them menu-based options would be better because that relies on recognition rather than recall.
which is a skilled task.
So, typically we should aim to design systems that support different user categories rather than specific categories.
Then rule number 3 says that we should offer informative feedback to the users.
Whatever action user does, some informative feedback should be given to the users.
For example, we are already familiar with the notion of progress bar.
When we install something or we do something, sometimes the progress bar appears to show the percentage of tasks completed.
So that is giving the user some sense of how much longer the user has to wait before the task completes.

Now, if we are not showing the progress bar, user will be at a loss to understand what the system is doing, whether the task is getting done or not, how much of the task gets completed and so on, that is not good for usable design.

Similarly, typically to save a file, we get to see that after the saving operation is done, if it is done successfully, then there is a color change on an image icon that shows a floppy disk, an earlier storage device instance.
It used to be the case in most desktop applications even a few years ago that there was a color change.
It still is there.
Now floppy, of course, is a storage metaphor representing the storage.
So before save there is one color; after the save operation is done there is another color.
Now this color change indicates that the save operation is done successfully.
Without this color change user will be not in a position to understand whether the save operation worked or not.
Then let us talk about rule number 4.
Design dialogues to yield closure.

So when user wants to achieve some objective, complete some tasks, the task, the system should be designed in a way such that the user gets a feeling that the task is started, executed and finally completed.
So some sort of dialogue should be there to indicate to the user that the task is now completed.
So that feedback is related, in fact, to the rule number 3 previous rule, and it advises the designer to organize activities into groups having a beginning part, middle part, and an end part.

you are expecting the user to perform a task to achieve some goal in your system, then that task execution should be designed in such a way that there is a beginning part of the task execution, middle part and a completion or end part.
And there should be some feedback at the end of each group.

Say, for example, in the case of online shopping, if you are doing a shopping activity, There are lots of subtasks, and then if there is some grouping like choosing items, putting them into the cart, and payment.

So, if you actually organize the subtasks into beginning, middle and end part, then it will be useful for the user to use the system and understand the working, how to proceed to achieve the objective.
So, it is always beneficial to have a system that is properly designed to let the user achieve a task with a clear-cut beginning part, middle part, and end part of the process.
Then there is rule number 5, which is to offer error prevention and simple error handling.
So, it is obvious and unavoidable that there will always be some error, as we are human, we all know.
So, error cannot be totally removed from our consideration.

However, we should try to have a design that lets the user make as few errors as possible so that we should design to keep error rates low. So, for example, Close and start options should not be kept close to each other.

So, if we are keeping the close option for an interface and the start option for the same interface side by side, then instead of closing, sometimes by mistake we can start it or instead of starting, sometimes by mistake we can close it.
So, that is of course one very simple trivial example of how to avoid errors, how to design to avoid error, to prevent errors.
But if error happens, we should not ideally show complicated messages to the user stating that there is some error.
Then that will confuse the user, that will scare the user.
Instead, the information should be simple, easy to understand language.
So rule 5 states that we offer error prevention in our design as well as something to handle errors if they happen.
In relation to this, there is another rule, rule 6, that is to permit easy reversal of actions.
So I have made some mistakes.
Now I want to rectify it.
So the reversal of action.
That led to the mistake that led to the error is an important design objective.
Ideally, we should keep the reversal option there so that users can come back from the erroneous situation.
So, you all have heard of the facilities called undo and redo.
These are primarily meant for that only, that is to permit easy reversal of action.
Rule 7 talks about keeping the users in control, that is letting the users feel that they are in control of the system.
So this feeling is very important otherwise the user will, because we are assuming the users are lay persons, they do not have much technical expertise.
So if we do not let this feeling go to the user then users will feel at a loss because Everything is very technical.
Users will not like to use the system and usability reduces.
So, users should be able to perceive their interaction.
They should be able to understand, perceive that something is happening.
And also, that something is happening means a change in system state.
The user should be able to perceive.
Say, for example, when the user is performing a drag and drop operation on a typical desktop application.

Then the user should be able to actually see that something is being dragged from one place to another and see, also see or visually perceive that when the object is dropped, then it is dropped at the place or it is being shown at the place where it is, where the user wants it to be, say maybe in another folder.
So, it should be shown there.
So, that is something that the user should be made aware of.
That the actions there should be feedback and the result of the actions there should be feedback.
Then we come to the last rule, that is, reduce short term memory load.
Now, this is a very interesting rule.
It came from psychological experiments.
So, our memory we can think of as comprising two parts in a very broad sense, short term and long term.
Short term memory is essentially a kind of notes.

So, when we perform some activities, we bring in some information from the long-term or permanent storage, long-term memory or permanent storage into the short-term memory which is non-permanent storage, just a kind of notebook sort of thing to aid our activities, day-to-day activities.

Now, the finding Originally proposed by George Miller way back in 1956, almost 70 years ago, says that, so the rule was the 7 plus or minus 2 rule, which says that at a time in our short-term memory, it is best to keep between 7 to 9, between 5 to 9 chunks of information.
That is our limit.
If we are trying to, of course, if we keep less, then we are underutilizing our memory, short term memory.
And if we are trying to keep more, then we are overutilizing.
So, keeping more is actually harmful.
So, if we want the user to remember a lot of things, recall a lot of things from long term memory to short term memory in order to make the interface usable.
Then certainly our physiology does not support that.
So, in that case, it is likely that the user will not be able to use it.
So, if we require more than 9 chunks of information to be utilized while operating an interface.
So, our objective should be to keep the information required to operate an interface or perform an interaction between 5 to 9 for optimum outcome by the user.
So, In short, we can say that we should not force users to remember too many things where too many in this context quantitatively we can call more than nine chunks of information.
Chunks of information is essentially a unit of information.
It can represent one letter, it can represent one word or a whole sentence as well or a whole concept.
It varies from application to application.
So, these are eight rules and as I said before, these are quite generic in nature.
They need not be specific to any product or any system.
However, as we can see, they can be applicable to a broad class of interactive systems, and you can analyze and see whether or how much of those are applicable to extended reality systems.
Now, let us move our focus to another aspect of design.
which we will be requiring in subsequent parts of this lecture, that is interaction techniques that are used in extended reality.
Our primary focus will be virtual reality.
Why do we need to know this?
Interaction in non-immersive settings such as AR is similar to interactions we are familiar with, such as touch, gesture, etc.
So, there is nothing significant here.
However, for immersive VR or MR experiences, specialized techniques and setups are used, and we should be aware of those in order to be able to properly design the experience.
So, it is important to know and use suitable interaction techniques for enhanced presence.
So, we need to know what kind of interactions are supported.

Now, there are different types of interactions that are typically designed for immersive environments, immersive experiences: one is object interaction, then navigation, and thirdly interaction for system control.
So, broadly three categories: object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment.

Navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment and thirdly, interaction for system control means several system-related settings interaction required to change those settings.
So, we will talk about these interaction types in a subsequent part of the lecture.
So, in summary, what we have discussed so far in this part of the lecture is we talked about the idea of design, particularly interface and interaction design.
We talked about design guidelines; that is the starting point.
The design language we will be talking about in the next lecture is a separate topic that is part of a separate topic.
We also briefly touched on the interaction techniques.
More details will be covered in the subsequent part of this lecture on design.
So, we will continue on these interaction techniques in a subsequent part.
So, I hope I could explain the topics in an easy-to-understand manner.
You are able to follow the concepts.
We talked about design, design guidelines, starting points and Shneiderman's eight golden rules, their applicability on extended reality systems and also started our discussion on interaction design.
So, we will continue our discussion.
Looking forward to meeting you in the next part of the lecture.
Till then, thank you, goodbye, and happy learning.

parts.objective: Describe interface and interaction design within the design stage of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle for immersive experiences

key_points.text: The interactive system development lifecycle (SDLC) includes stages such as feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis and specification, design, prototyping, evaluation, coding, testing, and deployment (7, 8, 9).
The overall design of an immersive experience involves the entire design-prototype-evaluate cycle to incorporate user requirements (26).
The interactive system development lifecycle (SDLC) includes two types of design stages: code design and system design (14, 18).

terms.name: Interactive system development lifecycle
terms.definition: The interactive system development lifecycle describes the stages used in developing a system, which includes feasibility study, requirement gathering, analysis, specification, the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, code design, coding and implementation, code testing, empirical study, and deployment and maintenance.

terms.name: Design-prototype-evaluate cycle
terms.definition: Design-prototype-evaluate cycle is a phase within the interactive system development lifecycle that comprises design, prototyping, and early evaluation to incorporate user requirements.

parts.objective: Analyze methods for starting the design process and utilize different design guidelines and specification languages

key_points.text: Interface and interaction design requires addressing two issues: where to start the design process and how to represent the resulting design using a design language. [30-32]
The design process can start with creative thinking aided by intuition, experience, or domain knowledge, or it can start with pre-existing guidelines, heuristics, or checklists. [35-43]
Design guidelines are categorized as generic (broad, high-level, applicable widely) or specific (detailed, covering micro aspects of a particular system). [45-55, 73-75]
Prototypes can be used as a language to express interface design ideas and constitute a specification of the design. [66-68]

terms.name: Design process
terms.definition: The design process is how one starts the design and how one represents what has been designed. It can start through creative thinking or through established guidelines.

terms.name: Design language
terms.definition: A design language is the method or set of rules needed to express a design, allowing ideas to be brainstormed or refined.

terms.name: Creative thinking process
terms.definition: This process is assumed to be a starting point for design and relies on creativity, which may be aided by intuition, experience, or domain knowledge.

terms.name: Eight golden rules by Shneiderman
terms.definition: This is a generic set of rules, primarily meant for graphical user interfaces, but its broad nature makes it applicable to other interactive systems.

terms.name: Seven principles by Norman
terms.definition: These principles were designed in the 1980s and were primarily meant for Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs), though they are generic enough to apply to other domains.

terms.name: Human interface guidelines
terms.definition: This is a specific set of guidelines originally developed by Apple to cover the minute aspects of their user interfaces.

terms.name: Specification of design
terms.definition: The specification of design is the formal documentation used to express whatever has been thought out in the design process.

terms.name: Specification of interface design
terms.definition: Specification of interface design is one of the design languages used to describe the interface of a system.

terms.name: Specification of code design
terms.definition: Specification of code design is one of the design languages used to describe the code of a system.

terms.name: Prototype
terms.definition: A prototype can be considered a language for interface design, functioning as a way to express design ideas.

terms.name: Cyber sickness
terms.definition: Cyber sickness is an issue that specific design guidelines are created to avoid or minimize, particularly in VR or immersive systems.

parts.objective: Explain Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules and their application to designing diverse interactive and extended reality systems

key_points.text: Shneiderman’s Eight Golden Rules, originally developed for GUIs, can be broadly applied to various interactive and extended reality systems.
Consistency is achieved through internal uniformity of design elements for the same tasks, and external alignment with real-world experience.
Designers must offer informative feedback, permit easy reversal of actions (undo/redo), and keep users in control of the system.
Interfaces should be designed for universal usability to accommodate all classes of users, and the information required to perform an interaction should be limited to between 5 and 9 chunks.

terms.name: Graphical user interface
terms.definition: A graphical user interface refers to a type of interface that the Eight Golden Rules were originally developed to apply to.

terms.name: Extended reality system
terms.definition: Extended reality systems are types of interfaces to which Shneiderman’s guidelines can be partly or fully applicable.

terms.name: Consistency
terms.definition: Consistency is a design requirement that dictates that when designing an interface, there must be a consistent pattern in the design.

terms.name: Internal consistency
terms.definition: Internal consistency means that for the same task, the same elements or interactions should be used across different parts of the design.

terms.name: External consistency
terms.definition: External consistency ensures that the elements and interactions in the system closely match the user's existing real-world experience and knowledge.

terms.name: Universal usability
terms.definition: Universal usability is a design principle requiring that the system provides adequate facilities for all classes of users, regardless of their experience level.

terms.name: Novice
terms.definition: A novice refers to a user who is engaging with the system for the very first time.

terms.name: Expert
terms.definition: An expert refers to a user who is highly frequent in their usage of the system, rather than an expert in technology itself.

terms.name: Recognition
terms.definition: Recognition is a method of interaction where the system relies on the user identifying presented options rather than recall, which is a skilled task.

terms.name: Informative feedback
terms.definition: Informative feedback requires that for whatever action a user performs in a system, some form of feedback must be provided to them.

terms.name: Progress bar
terms.definition: A progress bar is a graphical element that appears when a user is performing a task, like an installation, showing the percentage of the task that has been completed.

terms.name: Storage metaphor
terms.definition: A storage metaphor is a visual concept, such as a floppy disk, that represents the idea of storage, and changes (like a color change) can be used to indicate the status of a saving operation.

terms.name: Closure
terms.definition: Closure is a design rule where the system is structured so that the user feels a task has been started, executed, and finally completed.

terms.name: Feedback
terms.definition: Feedback is communication, such as a dialogue, designed to indicate to the user that a task has been completed or that the result of an action is being shown.

terms.surface: Beginning part, middle part, and end part
terms.name: Task execution
terms.definition: Task execution is a structured process organized into a beginning part, a middle part, and an end part to ensure the user understands the working and how to proceed.

terms.name: Subtask
terms.definition: Subtasks are the many smaller tasks that comprise a larger activity and can be organized into a beginning, middle, and end structure.

terms.name: Error prevention
terms.definition: Error prevention is a design practice aimed at minimizing the possibility of errors by designing the interface such that users make as few mistakes as possible.

terms.name: Easy reversal of action
terms.definition: Easy reversal of actions is an important design objective that provides the user with the ability to return from an erroneous situation or rectify a mistake they have made.

terms.name: Reversal of action
terms.definition: Reversal of action is a design objective that permits users to rectify mistakes by providing facilities such as undo and redo.

terms.name: Keeping the user in control
terms.definition: Keeping the user in control is a design goal that ensures users feel a sense of agency over the system, preventing them from feeling lost or overwhelmed by technical complexity.

terms.name: Change in system state
terms.definition: A change in system state is the realization that something is happening within the system, and the user should be able to perceive this change.

terms.name: Drag and drop operation
terms.definition: A drag and drop operation is a method where the user visually sees an object being moved from one area of the application to another and subsequently dropped in the desired location.

terms.name: Short term memory load
terms.definition: Short term memory load is a design rule that involves minimizing the amount of information a user must remember by keeping the required chunks between 5 and 9.

terms.name: Short term memory
terms.definition: Short term memory functions like a temporary notebook used during daily activities, holding non-permanent information temporarily. It is a component of memory that holds immediate information while we perform activities.

terms.name: Long term memory
terms.definition: Long term memory or permanent storage is where information is held permanently. Activities involve bringing information from this permanent storage into the short term memory.

terms.name: 7 plus or minus 2 rule
terms.definition: The 7 plus or minus 2 rule, originally proposed by George Miller, suggests that the optimal capacity for information held in short term memory is between 7 to 9 chunks.

terms.name: Chunk of information
terms.definition: A chunk of information is essentially a defined unit of information that can represent anything from a single letter or word to an entire sentence or concept, and its size varies by application.

parts.objective: Identify the specialized types of interaction techniques crucial for designing immersive VR and MR experiences

key_points.text: Interaction in AR environments is similar to familiar methods like touch and gesture, but immersive VR or MR experiences require specialized techniques for proper design and enhanced presence.
Immersive interactions are broadly categorized into three types: object interaction, navigation, and system control.

terms.name: Virtual reality
terms.definition: Virtual reality refers to immersive experiences that require specialized techniques and setups for interaction. The goal of using suitable interaction techniques in VR is to achieve enhanced presence.

terms.name: Object interaction
terms.definition: Object interaction is a type of interaction where a user selects and manipulates objects that are part of the virtual environment.

terms.name: Navigation
terms.definition: Navigation describes the action of moving from one point to another within the virtual environment.

terms.name: Interaction for system control
terms.definition: Interaction for system control refers to the interaction required to change various system-related settings within the immersive experience.

objectives.text: you'll be able to explain how to initiate a design process and describe interface and interaction design within the design-prototype-evaluate cycle
you'll be able to explain Shneiderman's Eight Golden Rules and apply them to designing diverse interactive and extended reality systems
you'll be able to identify the specialized types of interaction techniques crucial for designing immersive VR and MR experiences

lecture_goal: Develop the skills needed to plan, structure, and refine interfaces for effective immersive and extended reality experiences.
